intro_script: Welcome to your daily research digest for November 25th, 2026. Today we dive into agentic training, large-scale agent analysis, and clever prompt injection techniques. Here are ten stories to explore.
outro_script: And that's all for today's research digest. Hope you learned something fascinating about agentic learning! Go forth and learn something new. Until tomorrow, keep pondering those complex connections. Bye for now!

items.title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
items.summary: Agentic competence is decomposed into task competence, which is the knowledge to solve a task, and interface competence, which is the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Training methods interact differently with these two components, as single-harness training can interfere with interface competence. Harness rehearsal, combining task supervision with interface exposure, yields significantly larger gains than either method alone. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge, but its effectiveness depends on preserving or improving interface competence during training. Policy reinforcement learning is found to be more robust than distillation for single-harness training while maintaining interface competence across harnesses.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training" reports on the decomposition of agentic competence into task competence and interface competence and examines how different training methods affect these components. The research found that single-harness training can interfere with interface competence, and that harness rehearsal, which combines task supervision with interface exposure, results in significantly larger gains than either method in isolation. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge, with its effectiveness contingent upon maintaining or improving interface competence during training, while policy reinforcement learning demonstrated greater robustness than distillation for single-harness training while preserving interface competence across harnesses. This work provides a framework for optimizing agent training by explicitly managing the separation between knowing a task and executing actions within an interface.

items.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
items.summary: Taxi is a system designed for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents efficiently at scale, handling millions of steps. It primarily uses clustering to create a step taxonomy and provides full SQL access for complex querying by engineers and agents. The system employs a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent and incorporates Jev-style decision models for probabilistic routing. Taxi features an extensible ecosystem with built-in evaluators and modular design for easy integration. This framework aims to facilitate the analysis of large-scale agent behavior.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale" details a system designed for efficiently debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents across millions of steps. This work presents a framework utilizing clustering to establish a step taxonomy and providing full SQL access for complex querying of agent behavior. The system employs a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent and incorporates Jev-style decision models for probabilistic routing within its operational methodology. Taxi features an extensible ecosystem with built-in evaluators and a modular design intended to facilitate the comprehensive analysis of large-scale agent behavior. This framework represents a significant step in creating scalable methods for understanding complex autonomous system operations. Further developments in agent analysis are expected to follow this foundational work.

items.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
items.summary: Attackers can exploit benign conversation history to perform indirect prompt injection without altering prior turns. The ContextLure framework allows attackers to silently observe these conversations to extract evidence for injection. To effectively exploit this, the framework selects evidence based on user/system preferences and uses an urgency/priority matrix for constructing malicious requests. Evaluation showed that attackers can leverage this evidence to achieve successful injections in later attacks. Results indicate that attackers can use benign interaction evidence for attacks without poisoning the original conversation.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection". This report details a framework that enables attackers to perform indirect prompt injection by exploiting benign conversation history without altering prior turns. The ContextLure framework functions by silently observing conversations to extract necessary evidence for injection, utilizing user or system preferences and an urgency priority matrix to construct malicious requests. Evaluation demonstrated that attackers can leverage this benign interaction evidence to achieve successful injections in subsequent attacks, indicating that successful injections can occur without poisoning the original conversation. This research highlights a vulnerability in the security of conversational AI systems that requires further investigation into history management protocols.

items.title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
items.summary: The research investigates how adversarial names, tokens, and attack rewrites affect decision models like Laya, which provide probability outputs based on text and questions. Researchers executed 81 programmatic edits on six Laya models using 566 synthetic items to measure how successfully attackers hijack or lose correct answers. Findings indicate that naming an option steers the model (32%), while character edits cost up to 72% of correct answers in one version. Sanitizers proved ineffective against unseen generalizations, as an attacker could restore success to 84% by selecting the best manipulated strings. Label-free checks focused on option names showed strong performance for sentence attacks (AUROC 0.95).
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations" investigates how adversarial names, tokens, and attack rewrites affect decision models like Laya, finding that naming an option steers the model by thirty-two percent and character edits can cost up to seventy-two percent of correct answers in one version. Researchers executed eighty-one programmatic edits on six Laya models using five hundred sixty-six synthetic items to measure the success of hijacking or losing correct answers. Findings indicate that sanitizers proved ineffective against unseen generalizations, as an attacker could restore success to eighty-four percent by selecting the best manipulated strings, with label-free checks focusing on option names showing strong performance for sentence attacks. This research highlights vulnerabilities in current AI safety mechanisms against subtle textual manipulation.

items.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
items.summary: Spatial reasoning agents often struggle with orchestrating external tools for spatial tasks. SpatialCraft is a self-evolving framework that allows frozen agents to improve orchestration based on their interaction history. It maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, which are condition-action tactics, and Skills, which are multi-step procedures. Experiences are refined using a Contrastive Utility Score to isolate their true impact. SpatialCraft demonstrates superior accuracy across spatial benchmarks by learning to manage spatial tools from experience.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents" reports on a self-evolving framework designed to improve the orchestration of external tools for spatial reasoning agents based on their interaction history. The research details the SpatialCraft framework, which maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, defined as condition-action tactics, and Skills, which represent multi-step procedures. The system refines the Experiences using a Contrastive Utility Score to determine true impact, allowing frozen agents to learn better orchestration. Demonstrations show that SpatialCraft achieves superior accuracy across spatial benchmarks by learning how to manage spatial tools through accumulated experience. This development indicates a pathway for agents to enhance complex interaction capabilities through experiential learning. Future research will focus on scaling this procedural intelligence across more complex environments.

items.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
items.summary: Existing benchmarks for MLLMs often focus only on coarse-grained emotion or binary truth-deception detection. This research introduces InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark designed to assess fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. It identifies six specific manipulation strategies, including withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. A multi-agent annotation framework is developed to create reliable labels from contextual evidence for this benchmark. The work provides a testbed for evaluating models on nuanced understanding of conversational information manipulation.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations" introduces InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark designed to assess fine-grained information manipulation within conversations. The research identifies six specific manipulation strategies including withholding leakage fabrication evasion and defensive counterclaim. A multi-agent annotation framework was developed to generate reliable labels from contextual evidence for this benchmark. This work provides a testbed for evaluating models on nuanced understanding of conversational information manipulation through its structured assessment of subtle conversational alterations. The development signals a necessary shift in evaluation methods for multimodal large language models.

items.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
items.summary: The Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model is proposed to address attribute reduction in incomplete information systems by handling missing values differently than standard rough set theory. It defines object similarity based on a weighted overlap of present attributes, penalizing missing values globally. A soft dependency degree is derived from this similarity, and reducts are found using greedy backward elimination in $O(|U|^2 |A|^2)$ time. Experimental results show COFRS yields the smallest reducts on average across various benchmarks with missing data. While COFRS is not superior in predictive accuracy for some classifiers, it offers a gain in compactness.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data" presents a model designed to address attribute reduction in incomplete information systems by handling missing values differently than standard rough set theory, demonstrating that the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set model yields the smallest reducts on average across various benchmarks with missing data. The research introduces the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set model which defines object similarity based on a weighted overlap of present attributes, penalizing missing values globally to derive a soft dependency degree. Reductions are subsequently found using a greedy backward elimination process that operates in time proportional to the square of the universe size and the attribute size. Experimental evaluations indicate that while the model does not necessarily achieve superior predictive accuracy for certain classifiers, it provides a measurable gain in model compactness. This work suggests a new framework for data reduction in environments characterized by missing information.

items.title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
items.summary: Existing benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) focus primarily on static chart-to-code generation, neglecting interactive chart exploration. ChartInt is introduced as a new benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation, including common interaction patterns like hovering and data updates. A preset state snapshot protocol is proposed to enable reproducible evaluation of dynamic interaction behaviors. The framework measures semantic and stylistic consistency during these interactive tasks. Experiments demonstrate that MLLMs perform poorly on interactive tasks compared to static chart generation.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs" presents a new benchmark focusing on interactive chart-to-code generation for multimodal large language models. ChartInt is introduced as a benchmark designed to evaluate interactive chart exploration, including interaction patterns such as hovering and data updates, utilizing a preset state snapshot protocol to ensure reproducible evaluation of dynamic interaction behaviors. The framework measures semantic and stylistic consistency during these interactive tasks, and experiments indicate that multimodal large language models perform less effectively on these interactive tasks when compared to static chart generation. This research suggests that future benchmarks must incorporate dynamic interaction evaluation to accurately assess the capabilities of multimodal large language models in data visualization tasks.

items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
items.summary: MOZAIC is a paired benchmark designed to assess audio-video deepfakes by providing four-way labels detailing the real/fake status of both video and audio modalities. It evaluates fakes involving inner-face swapping, video diffusion, and voice conversion, using 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs. The benchmark includes tasks for authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation. Evaluation shows that multimodal LLMs achieve 35.6% on the primary task, and detectors reach 98.4% accuracy on authenticity. The work also releases the dataset and the MOZAIC-SMALL split.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake" details a paired benchmark designed to assess audio-video deepfakes using four-way labels for real or fake status across both modalities. The research utilized 137,745 clips derived from 15,014 source pairs to evaluate manipulations involving inner-face swapping, video diffusion, and voice conversion. The benchmark incorporates tasks focusing on authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation. Evaluation results indicate that multimodal large language models achieved thirty-five point six percent on the primary task, while detectors demonstrated ninety-eight point four percent accuracy in assessing authenticity. The study also releases the full dataset and a smaller split known as MOZAIC-SMALL. This work provides a quantitative measure for detecting sophisticated audio-video manipulations in artificial media.

items.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
items.summary: Allocation is presented as a structural component of autonomous agent governance, not just an auxiliary concern. Allocation mechanisms introduce trade-offs among fairness, efficiency, and strategic resistance when agents compete for resources. These constraints propagate across system dimensions including execution atomicity, state enforcement, behavioral drift, and population allocation. An irreducibility theorem proves that no single governance layer can resolve these dimensions without sacrificing correctness or stability. Consequently, agent governance is reframed as a structural problem concerning how execution access is determined.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition" presents a framework for autonomous agent systems focusing on allocation mechanisms that introduce trade-offs among fairness, efficiency, and strategic resistance. The research establishes an irreducibility theorem demonstrating that no single governance layer can resolve these multi-dimensional constraints without sacrificing correctness or stability. The methodology reframes agent governance as a structural problem centered on how execution access is determined, showing how allocation mechanisms impose constraints across execution atomicity, state enforcement, behavioral drift, and population allocation. This finding indicates that designing robust agent systems requires addressing these interconnected resource allocation dimensions simultaneously. The implications suggest a shift toward structural design principles for ensuring reliable and fair autonomous agent interactions in future systems.
